About us

Who are we? The Social Investment Agency leads the implementation of social investment and provide cross-sector insights to decision-makers to improve people’s lives. Ultimately, we want our approaches to achieve sustainable improvements for New Zealanders. We welcome feedback, questions and ideas from our followers but we can’t guarantee we will reply individually to every post. If you have an urgent query, please contact us directly, https://www.sia.govt.nz/about/contact-us/ . Comments and tagged content are monitored during business hours, from 9am to 5pm Monday through Friday. While we will attempt to answer all questions, we cannot enter into discussion related to politics. We will review replies and comments made to us and pass any emerging themes or suggestions to relevant people in the agency. We reserve the right to remove any post or comment that does not comply with the social media service’s Terms of Service or user agreement. In addition, we may remove content that is not relevant; is deemed offensive; includes misinformation, swearing or hate speech; has political bias; or includes advertising. Please be respectful to us and to others. If harmful or irrelevant content is repeatedly posted, you may be blocked.

    Over the past year, we've been working with communities, iwi and social service providers to back approaches that support people earlier, more effectively, and with a stronger focus on outcomes.   Through the Social Investment Fund, we're partnering with organisations that have the scale and capability to help test new ways of funding social services. The goal is to learn what works and create approaches that can be adopted more widely across government.    Less complexity. More flexibility. Better use of data. We're exploring how government and social service organisations can work differently to achieve better outcomes for people, families and whānau.

    Social investment is about proving what works and supporting better decisions with data and evidence. Here at the Social Investment Agency, we’ve developed a repeatable analysis that uses existing government data to generate insights we can apply across different groups. This approach helps us: - understand people’s experiences - compare outcomes across groups - support more targeted, effective support. Because it’s repeatable and standardised, we can deliver more insights with less effort over time, helping organisations who provide social services act earlier, target better, and improve outcomes. By publishing our methodology, we're giving other agencies a proven, repeatable approach to producing consistent, scalable insights that support better decisions. Find our Standardised Cohort Analysis Methodology Overview here: https://lnkd.in/ecQkZkqr

    Trust and relationships. Those were two key themes that came through during Government Innovation Week, an event designed to create a dialogue on improving service outcomes and creating a more connected government that is easier to navigate. Our AI Lead, Ernestynne Walsh, participated in two panels on data sovereignty and redesigning processes. Her key messages included the importance of iwi and Māori data sovereignty as well as building relationships with others to help redesign services. Pictured are panel members (left to right) Bill Moses, NZQA; Ben Sheehan, Technology One; Ernestynne Walsh, SIA; and Kari Jones, FMA.

    Communities know what works for their people.   Expressions of Interest are now open for local groups who want to lead the design of a community‑led commissioning approach for their area, working alongside government. This is an opportunity to take the lead—bringing your knowledge, relationships, lived experience, and local data together to shape solutions that reflect your community’s values, priorities and aspirations.   This is about you and your community: - leading decisions that affect your people - designing solutions grounded in local knowledge and relationships - acting on what you already know works in your community - accessing and using data and evidence to support decision-making - creating approaches that are trusted, sustainable and shaped locally.   You bring the insight, commitment and connection. This work is about backing your leadership, so solutions are designed by those who know best.   If you’re part of a committed group of local leaders ready to work together and shape how services support your community, we want to hear from you.   Find out more and apply here: https://lnkd.in/e4EYj4Sy

    Today, SIA staff welcomed Brendan Boyle through a whakatau, marking the start of his role as Acting Secretary for Social Investment and Chief Executive of the Social Investment Agency. Many will already know Brendan as a senior public sector leader with extensive experience across social policy, regulation, governance, digital technology, and service delivery in large and complex organisations. He has previously held Chief Executive roles at the Ministry of Social Development, the Department of Internal Affairs, and Land Information New Zealand, and most recently served as Acting Chief Executive of Pharmac. We’re looking forward to continuing to build impact and improve outcomes for New Zealanders under Brendan’s leadership.

    Thanks Social Value Aotearoa for sharing these highlights. When commissioning social services, it is important to get the foundations right - starting with the RFP. To be successful, organisations need to understand what is required to deliver on their theory of change. Under the Social Investment Fund, we are spending time upfront with organisations to ensure they are well placed to deliver the best possible outcomes. Joe Fowler

    Social Value Aotearoa

    2,127 followers

    2mo

    Why underpriced services lead to failure - a striking reflection from Joe Fowler, Social Investment Agency, during our panel on Investing in What Works: The Economics of Social Value. Joe drew on years of commissioning experience across New Zealand and the UK - and named a pattern that holds the sector back: organisations underpricing their services just to win contracts, often leaving themselves unable to deliver on their own theory of change. His message was clear. The real question isn't "what price will get us across the line?" It's "what does it actually cost to make this work?" A valuable reminder that true value for money starts with understanding what delivery really requires.
